blocks.orig: Lake Eyasi is a seasonal shallow endorheic salt lake on the floor of the Great Rift Valley. It is in northern Tanzania, south of the Ngorongoro highlands. You will have plenty of time to enjoy this tranquil environment and to absorb its natural setting. This large lake lays hight above sea level. In contrast to the savannah and arid plains of  northern national parks, Lake Eyasi offers tall palm trees along its shores.
blocks.html: Set on the floor of the Great Rift Valley, Lake Eyasi is a shallow salt lake with no outflow that fills and shrinks with the seasons. It lies in the north of Tanzania, just below the Ngorongoro highlands. Here there is ample room to slow down, enjoy the quiet and let the scenery sink in. The lake is big and sits at considerable altitude. Whereas the parks further north consist of savannah and dry plains, tall palms line the shores of Lake Eyasi.

blocks.orig: Lake Eyasi doesn’t attract big-game wildlife populations as seen in the neighbouring parks and conservation areas, you won’t see the big five here. The lake is a birdwatchers dream due to the many resident species of birds found here. The shallow waters support a huge diversity of breeding waterbirds from June to November. The main attraction are the large populations of flamingos and great white pelicans. Africa spoonbill, Fischer’s lovebird, gray headed gulls, pied avocet, spurfowl, stork, barbet, weaver and many more birds can be found around the shores of Lake Eyasi.
blocks.html: The big-game populations of the neighbouring parks and conservation areas are absent at Lake Eyasi, so don’t expect the big five here. What the lake does offer is a paradise for birdwatchers, thanks to the many bird species that live here permanently. Between June and November the shallow water supports an enormous variety of breeding waterbirds. The main draw are the big flocks of flamingos and great white pelicans. Along the shores you may also come across African spoonbill, Fischer’s lovebird, grey-headed gulls, pied avocet, spurfowl, stork, barbet, weaver and plenty of other species.

blocks.orig: Another great sighting are the many hippos at Lake Eyasi. The lake is providing them a place to avoid the hot sun during daytime. They are known to come and cool off in its brackish waters when the lake is full. A number of other wildlife species frequent the springs in the surrounding region.
blocks.html: The many hippos at Lake Eyasi are another fine sight. During the day the lake gives them somewhere to escape the fierce sun, and when the water level is high they are known to come and cool down in its brackish water. Various other wildlife species also visit the springs in the surrounding area.

blocks.orig: The Hadzabe bushmen live in the region around the lake. They are one of the few remaining tribes that still live the same way like they did hundreds of years ago. A visit with the bushmen is worthwhile! They subsist entirely of the bush and by bow hunting. The Hazabe Bushmen are one of the last remaining hunter-gatherers in Africa and live solely on the land. Just as in the Stone Age, like our ancestors did for thousands of years.
blocks.html: Around the lake live the Hadzabe bushmen, one of the few remaining tribes whose way of life has barely changed in hundreds of years. Paying them a visit is well worth it. They live entirely off the bush and hunt with bow and arrow. As one of the last hunter-gatherer peoples in Africa, the Hadzabe depend completely on the land, much as our ancestors did in the Stone Age for thousands of years.

blocks.orig: Besides the Hadzabe bushmen, you can also find the Datoga and Mbulu tribes here. A visit with the bushmen is worthwhile and they will graciously show you where and how they live and hunt. They subsist entirely of the bush and by bow hunting. The Hazabe Bushmen are one of the last remaining hunter-gatherers in Africa and live solely on the land. Just as in the Stone Age, like our ancestors did for thousands of years.
blocks.html: Alongside the Hadzabe bushmen, the Datoga and Mbulu tribes also live in this area. A visit to the bushmen is worthwhile: they will kindly show you where and how they live and hunt. They draw everything they need from the bush and hunt with bow and arrow. The Hadzabe are among the last hunter-gatherers left in Africa and live purely from the land, in the same way our ancestors did in the Stone Age for thousands of years.

blocks.orig: Experience the culture, habitat and way of life of the Hadzabe Bushmen first hand on this cultural activity. You go with the Bushman on a hunting trip around Lake Eyasi early in the morning. Learn how they make fire and prepare their food. In the afternoon you will visit a market where Hadzabe trade their honey, fruits and other things for knives, arrows and spears that the Datoga silversmith’s make. This cultural activity is absolutely a memorable experience and worth the extra time.
blocks.html: On this cultural activity you get to see the culture, habitat and daily life of the Hadzabe bushmen with your own eyes. Early in the morning you join the bushmen on a hunt around Lake Eyasi, and you find out how they light a fire and prepare their food. In the afternoon there is a visit to a market where the Hadzabe exchange honey, fruit and other goods for the knives, arrows and spears made by the Datoga silversmiths. It is a memorable activity and definitely worth setting aside the extra time for.

My name is Richard and I am a safari guide for 11 years at Lake Eyasi.
The Lake doesn’t attract many animals, but our clients enjoy the hippos and of course the flamingos. Many guest take part in hunting and learn some interesting skills from the Hadzabe.
blocks.html:
I am Richard, and I have worked as a safari guide at Lake Eyasi for 11 years.
Animals are not plentiful at the lake, but our clients do enjoy the hippos and, naturally, the flamingos. Many guests join a hunt and pick up some interesting skills from the Hadzabe.

blocks.orig: Which hotel? Our guests like Lake Eyasi Safari Lodge due friendly staff and the stunning views.
blocks.html: Where to stay? Lake Eyasi Safari Lodge is a favourite among our guests, thanks to the welcoming team and the superb views.

blocks.orig: The lake can be visited all year round. Lake Eyasi experiences a dry season from June to October and two rainy seasons which transform the landscape into a lush expanse of grasses. The short rains occur in November and December with sporadic showers and the longer rains occur from middle of March to May. Walking trails and roads will be effected by heavy rains, so it might impact the ease of for your travel.
blocks.html: You can visit the lake at any time of year. Lake Eyasi has a dry season from June to October, plus two rainy seasons that turn the landscape into a lush expanse of grass. The short rains fall in November and December as scattered showers, while the long rains last from mid-March to May. Heavy rain affects the walking trails and roads, which can make getting around less easy.

blocks.orig: Lake Eyasi is a seasonal shallow salt lake on the floor of the Great Rift which attracts hippos that like to cool off in its brackish waters. The area is home to the Hadzabe bushmen that will take you on a hunt. It is also a great place for bird lovers to spot flamingos, great white pelicans and many more.
blocks.html: Shallow and seasonal, the salt lake of Eyasi sits on the floor of the Great Rift, and hippos come here to cool down in its brackish water. The Hadzabe bushmen who live nearby will take you along on a hunt. Birders will find it a fine spot too, with flamingos, great white pelicans and plenty of other species to spot.
